title: What is the difference between method hiding (static) and method overriding (instance), and how does the resolution mechanism differ (compile-time reference type vs runtime object type)?
shortTitle: What is method hiding vs method overriding?

s1_definition.profdef: METHOD OVERRIDING (instance methods): child redefines a parent's instance method. Resolution at RUNTIME — the JVM checks the ACTUAL OBJECT TYPE in the heap and dispatches to the correct version (dynamic dispatch via vtable). `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` → `ref.calculateInterest()` calls SavingsAccount's version. METHOD HIDING (static methods): child defines a static method with the same signature as the parent's static method. Resolution at COMPILE TIME — the compiler checks the VARIABLE TYPE (reference type) and binds to that class's static method. `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` → `ref.getPolicy()` calls Account's version (because `ref` is declared as `Account`). Hiding is NOT polymorphism — no dynamic dispatch. The child's static method simply HIDES (shadows) the parent's in the child's namespace.
s1_definition.analogy: OVERRIDING: Rajesh calls the customer service number. The system checks his ACTUAL account type at runtime — routes to SavingsAccount team. Same number, different handler based on who's calling. HIDING: the bank's WEBSITE shows the standard policy page. If you navigate to the Savings Division's website, you see THEIR policy page. But if you use the main bank URL (parent reference), you ALWAYS see the main page — the website doesn't check your account type. It shows the page based on WHICH URL (reference type) you used.
s1_definition.oneliner: Overriding (instance): runtime dispatch based on ACTUAL object type. Hiding (static): compile-time binding based on REFERENCE type. Overriding = polymorphism. Hiding = NO polymorphism.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** METHOD OVERRIDING (instance methods): child redefines a parent's instance method. Resolution at RUNTIME — the JVM checks the ACTUAL OBJECT TYPE in the heap and dispatches to the correct version (dynamic dispatch via vtable). `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` → `ref.calculateInterest()` calls SavingsAccount's version. METHOD HIDING (static methods): child defines a static method with the same signature as the parent's static method. Resolution at COMPILE TIME — the compiler checks the VARIABLE TYPE (reference type) and binds to that class's static method. `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` → `ref.getPolicy()` calls Account's version (because `ref` is declared as `Account`). Hiding is NOT polymorphism — no dynamic dispatch. The child's static method simply HIDES (shadows) the parent's in the child's namespace.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** OVERRIDING: Rajesh calls the customer service number. The system checks his ACTUAL account type at runtime — routes to SavingsAccount team. Same number, different handler based on who's calling. HIDING: the bank's WEBSITE shows the standard policy page. If you navigate to the Savings Division's website, you see THEIR policy page. But if you use the main bank URL (parent reference), you ALWAYS see the main page — the website doesn't check your account type. It shows the page based on WHICH URL (reference type) you used.

**One line to remember:** Overriding (instance): runtime dispatch based on ACTUAL object type. Hiding (static): compile-time binding based on REFERENCE type. Overriding = polymorphism. Hiding = NO polymorphism.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — A developer assumed static methods work polymorphically.** The bank's reporting service calls `account.getPolicy()` expecting different policies for different account types. For SavingsAccount: "4% interest, Rs.1000 min balance." For CurrentAccount: "Overdraft up to Rs.100K." But because getPolicy() is static and the reference type is Account, ALL accounts show "Standard Banking Policy" — the report is WRONG. The fix: make getPolicy() an INSTANCE method (override works) OR call the static via the class name explicitly.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `Account ref = new SavingsAccount("SAV001", 125000)`. Variable type: Account. Actual object: SavingsAccount.

**Step 2 — Instance method (overriding).** `ref.getDescription()`. Compiler: "Account has getDescription() — valid call." Runtime: JVM checks heap — actual type is SavingsAccount → dispatches to SavingsAccount.getDescription() → "Savings Account (4% interest, min Rs.1000)". RUNTIME dispatch.

**Step 3 — Static method (hiding).** `ref.getPolicy()`. Compiler: "ref is Account. Account has static getPolicy(). Bind to Account.getPolicy()." No runtime check. → "Standard Banking Policy". COMPILE-TIME binding. Even though the object IS SavingsAccount, static ignores the actual type.

**Step 4 — Change reference.** `SavingsAccount saRef = (same object)`. `saRef.getPolicy()` → compiler sees SavingsAccount → binds to SavingsAccount.getPolicy() → "Savings Policy." SAME object, DIFFERENT reference type → DIFFERENT static result. Proves: static = reference type binding.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ OVERRIDING (instance method) — RUNTIME dispatch ═══

  Account ref = new SavingsAccount(...);
  ref.getDescription();
    │
    COMPILER: Account has getDescription()? YES → valid call (Recommended) 
    │
    RUNTIME (JVM): actual type in heap = SavingsAccount
    → vtable lookup → SavingsAccount.getDescription()
    → "Savings Account (4% interest)"

  ═══ HIDING (static method) — COMPILE-TIME binding ═══

  Account ref = new SavingsAccount(...);
  ref.getPolicy();
    │
    COMPILER: ref type = Account → bind to Account.getPolicy()
    → "Standard Banking Policy"
    │
    NO RUNTIME CHECK! Actual object type IGNORED!

  ═══ COMPARISON ═══

  Feature    │ OVERRIDING (instance)       │ HIDING (static)
  ───────────│─────────────────────────────│─────────────────────────
  Method     │ Instance (non-static)       │ Static
  Resolution │ RUNTIME (object type)       │ COMPILE-TIME (ref type)
  Mechanism  │ vtable dynamic dispatch     │ Direct class binding
  Polymorphic│ YES (Recommended) │ NO (Avoid) 
  @Override  │ YES — compiler verifies     │ NO — just shadowing
```

```
  ┌──────────────┐   calcFee()    ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Txn Service  │ ─────────────▶ │  FeeCalculator    │
  └──────────────┘                │  (base type)      │
                                  └─────────┬─────────┘
             instance override (RUNTIME)    │
                ┌───────────────────────────┼───────────────────┐
                ▼                           ▼                    ▼
        ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
        │ SavingsFee   │          │ CurrentFee   │     │ NriFee       │
        │ override     │          │ override     │     │ override     │
        └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘

  Instance methods → dynamic dispatch → correct subtype at RUNTIME.
  Static methods (e.g. version()) → resolved by COMPILE-TIME type →
  no polymorphism → the declared reference type wins. (hiding, not override)

  DB stores fee rules; audit log records which concrete calculator ran.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Method overriding applies to instance methods and uses RUNTIME dispatch: the JVM checks the actual object type in the heap and calls the correct version. `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` → `ref.getDescription()` calls SavingsAccount's version because the JVM dispatches based on the actual type. Method hiding applies to static methods and uses COMPILE-TIME binding: the compiler looks at the reference variable type and binds directly. `ref.getPolicy()` calls Account's version because the compiler sees `ref` is declared as Account — it NEVER checks the actual object.

In my report service, the developer called `account.getPolicy()` through an Account reference expecting different policies per type. ALL accounts showed "Standard Banking Policy" — because getPolicy() is static and resolves at compile time to Account's version. The fix: either make getPolicy() an instance method (enables polymorphism) or call via class name (`SavingsAccount.getPolicy()`) which makes it explicit.

The proof: same object, different reference type → different static result. `Account ref = sa` → `ref.getPolicy()` = "Standard." `SavingsAccount saRef = sa` → `saRef.getPolicy()` = "Savings." The OBJECT didn't change — only the REFERENCE TYPE changed. This proves static methods bind at compile time to the reference type. Instance methods bind at runtime to the actual object type. This is why static methods are HIDDEN, not OVERRIDDEN — and why calling static methods on instance references is a code smell.
